stories.headline: S&P 500, NASDAQ-100 SLIDE AS AI-REVENUE DOUBTS HIT MEGA-CAP TECH
stories.body: The S&P 500 fell 0.47% to 7,765 and the Nasdaq-100 dropped 1.39% to 30,726 after a Financial Times report cast doubt on OpenAI's revenue trajectory, dragging Nvidia, Micron, and Intel lower; the Dow Jones bucked the trend, adding roughly 0.1% as money rotated into value names outside the AI trade. Markets are closed for the weekend with no new catalyst to move these levels.
stories.explain: Mega-cap AI suppliers trade on a long-duration growth story: today's price embeds years of assumed compute demand from a small number of customers, chief among them OpenAI, so any doubt about that demand materializing resets the present value of distant cash flows disproportionately hard. The Dow's gain while the Nasdaq-100 fell shows the selling is concentrated rotation out of AI-exposed names rather than a broad risk-off move, which matters because the two patterns call for very different responses from investors.

stories.headline: OIL CLIMBS ON REPORTS OF POTENTIAL U.S. STRIKES ON IRAN AS 10-YEAR YIELD HOLDS NEAR 2007 HIGHS
stories.body: WTI crude rose 1.26% to roughly $91 a barrel after reports that the Pentagon is preparing contingency options for potential military action against Iran, while the 10-year Treasury yield eased 5 basis points to 5.23% but remains close to its highest level since 2007. No fresh de-escalation or escalation headlines broke over the weekend.
stories.explain: Oil's move is a geopolitical risk premium, not a demand story: traders price in the probability that an escalation could disrupt tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, so the barrel price rises even before any actual supply is lost. The 10-year's stickiness near 5.2% compounds the tech selloff because it raises the discount rate applied to exactly the kind of long-duration cash flows the AI trade depends on, so elevated yields and AI-revenue doubts are pulling on the same valuation lever from different directions.

stories.headline: GOVERNMENT FUNDED THROUGH DEC. 11 AS FY27 APPROPRIATIONS FIGHT STALLS IN THE SENATE
stories.body: The government remains funded through December 11 under the continuing resolution President Trump signed September 2 (House vote: 370-48), but none of the twelve FY2027 appropriations bills have yet been taken up by the Senate Appropriations Committee, setting up a funding cliff just after the midterm elections.
stories.explain: A continuing resolution freezes spending at prior-year levels rather than passing new appropriations, which avoids an immediate shutdown but pushes the harder fights over specific agency funding levels down the calendar. Punting the fight to right after the midterms raises the stakes because the incoming Congress's composition could change the bargaining leverage on both sides, and unresolved appropriations uncertainty is itself a small drag on Treasury issuance planning and the term premium investors demand for holding long bonds.

stories.headline: DOLLAR DIPS, GOLD HOLDS NEAR $4,160 AS HAVEN DEMAND NETS OUT FLAT
stories.body: The DXY slipped 0.11% to 102.11 while gold held essentially flat near $4,160 an ounce, as safe-haven demand tied to the Iran headlines roughly offset the dollar's own modest pullback. Both figures carry over unchanged into the weekend since currency and metals desks are quiet until Monday.
stories.explain: Gold and the dollar are both haven assets that usually move in opposite directions because gold is priced in dollars, so a weaker dollar should mechanically lift gold's price for dollar-based buyers. The flat gold price despite the softer dollar suggests the geopolitical bid for gold specifically is roughly balanced against reduced haven demand for the dollar itself, a sign investors aren't yet treating the Iran headlines as a major escalation.

stories.headline: ST. JOHN'S DEALS WITH FREEMAN'S SEASON-ENDING INJURY AS PRESEASON TAKES SHAPE AHEAD OF NOV. 2 TIP-OFF
stories.body: Rising junior guard Donnie Freeman remains out for all of 2026-27 after Achilles surgery, and coach Rick Pitino is still restructuring the Red Storm's rotation around the loss heading into Big East play in November. Nationally, preseason camps are in full swing with the men's season set to open Nov. 2; NCAA.com's preseason breakdown continues to flag Arkansas freshman Jordan Smith Jr. and Kansas freshman Tyran Stokes among the most-watched newcomers.

stories.headline: LEBRON JAMES DEALING WITH CHRONIC ARTHRITIS AND SCIATICA AHEAD OF SIXERS DEBUT
stories.body: ESPN's Dave McMenamin reports the 41-year-old James is managing chronic arthritis in his left foot plus ongoing sciatica as he enters his first season with Philadelphia; he sat out the Sixers' Oct. 5 preseason opener against the Knicks alongside Joel Embiid as a precaution. Elsewhere in the preseason, Dillon Brooks and John Collins scuffled in a heated opener, and Wizards center Alex Sarr is recovering from foot surgery and expected ready for opening night; the Sixers' real test comes Oct. 20 at Madison Square Garden.

stories.headline: FALCONS' PEARCE SUSPENSION AND YORK DISCIPLINE REVIEW LOOM AS SEAHAWKS HOST 49ERS SUNDAY
stories.body: Atlanta's eight-game suspension of edge rusher James Pearce Jr. for a personal-conduct violation and the league's ongoing review of 49ers owner Jed York following his Ohio arrest remain the NFL's biggest off-field storylines. On the field, Seattle (3-1) hosts an unbeaten San Francisco team Sunday at 4:25 p.m. ET at Lumen Field in a game with first-place NFC West implications.

stories.headline: NO. 1 TEXAS VISITS OKLAHOMA IN RED RIVER RIVALRY AS WASHINGTON FALLS 41-24 TO IOWA
stories.body: Top-ranked Texas and Oklahoma meet in the 123rd Red River Rivalry at the Cotton Bowl in Dallas (3:30 p.m. ET, ABC), the headline game of a Saturday slate that also features Georgia at Alabama in prime time. Washington's own Friday night game went the other way: No. 20 Iowa routed the Huskies 41-24 at Husky Stadium, building a 27-0 halftime lead behind Kamari Moulton's career-high 208 rushing yards, dropping UW to 3-3 (0-3 Big Ten).

sports.detail: Fell to No. 20 Iowa 41-24 at Husky Stadium Friday night, trailing 27-0 at halftime as Kamari Moulton ran for a career-high 208 yards and two touchdowns; UW's rushing attack was held to -3 yards. Washington drops to 3-3 (0-3 Big Ten). Next: at Purdue, Friday, Oct. 16, 5 p.m. PT (FOX) — UW's first trip to Purdue since 1990 — before a bye week Oct. 24.

UW released tip-off times for most of its 2026-27 slate. Nine new players are competing for roles after losing top scorers Hannes Steinbach (NBA Draft, Charlotte) and Zoom Diallo (transferred to Kentucky). Next: exhibition at Boise State Oct. 17 (6 p.m. PT), hosts rival Washington State Oct. 25 (1 p.m. PT), then opens the regular season at home vs. Colgate Nov. 2 and returns to the Maui Invitational (first time since 2010) Nov. 23 vs. BYU.

Beat the Chargers 30-23 to improve to 3-1, blowing a 30-13 third-quarter lead down to the wire before holding on. Sam Darnold threw for 168 yards and two touchdowns and jumped 51 spots to No. 21 in the NFL's new Top 100 rankings. Next: host unbeaten San Francisco Sunday, Oct. 11, 4:25 p.m. ET at Lumen Field (FOX) — first place in the NFC West on the line.

Beat Phoenix 109-91 in their preseason opener at Little Caesars Arena; Cade Cunningham led with 25 points and 12 rebounds. Center Jalen Duren signed a fully guaranteed five-year, $200 million deal Oct. 2, ending his restricted free-agency standoff and rejoining the roster for camp. Next: at Washington Wizards tonight, Oct. 10, 7 p.m. ET; regular-season opener is Oct. 20 vs. Boston.

Finished the season 76-86, missing the playoffs for the first time since 2019 — a stunning reversal after last year's Game 7 ALCS run. Manager Dan Wilson and four assistant coaches are out; president of baseball ops Jerry Dipoto says the club "will go outside to hire our manager" and is targeting someone with major-league managing experience, with Torey Lovullo off the board after re-signing with Arizona. No timetable has been set on the search.

deepDive.title: Term Premium: Why a 10-Year Yield Near 2007 Highs Hits Stocks Harder Than a Fed Hike Does
content: Today's brief carries over a detail easy to skim past: the 10-year Treasury yield eased slightly to 5.23% but remains near its highest level since 2007. That's not simply "rates are high" — it reflects something specific happening underneath the headline number, and it's the same number quietly weighing on the AI-stock selloff and the oil-driven risk premium sitting elsewhere in this brief. For a finance student, the 10-year yield is really two things stacked on top of each other: the market's expectation for where short-term rates average out over the next decade, plus a term premium investors demand for the extra risk of holding a longer-dated bond.

Term premium is compensation for uncertainty that a short-term rate expectation alone doesn't capture: the risk that inflation runs hotter than forecast, that the Treasury issues more debt than buyers want to absorb at current prices, or that a fiscal fight like the one over FY2027 appropriations drags on and clouds the outlook for future issuance. When that premium rises, the 10-year yield can climb even if the Fed itself isn't actively hiking — which is close to today's situation, where yields are elevated less because of imminent policy moves and more because investors want extra compensation for holding duration amid geopolitical risk and funding uncertainty.

The mechanical point that matters for equities is discounting: every dollar of future corporate earnings gets converted to today's price using a discount rate built on the risk-free yield plus an equity risk premium. A 10-year yield near 5.2% is roughly double what it was for most of the 2010s, which means the same dollar of earnings five or ten years out is worth meaningfully less today than it was when yields sat near 2%. Growth stocks priced on earnings far in the future — the AI-capex names at the center of today's Nasdaq-100 selloff — are the most exposed to this math, because their valuation case leans hardest on cash flows that discounting punishes most severely as yields climb.

The practical read for a portfolio: watch whether next week's data and the appropriations fight push the term premium higher or let it ease. A resolution that removes fiscal uncertainty, or a Fed path that looks more credible on inflation, would let the term-premium component of the 10-year shrink even without rate cuts, and that alone could support a bounce in exactly the long-duration AI names that sold off this week. Conversely, if the funding cliff after the midterms starts looking disorderly, expect the 10-year to test fresh multi-decade highs — and expect that pressure to show up first in the stocks priced furthest out on the growth curve, not in the broad index.
